title: What Is PPP and Why Does It Matter?
brief: Introduce the Presentation-Practice-Production framework as a three-stage lesson structure. Draw on the module's descriptions of teacher-led vocabulary introduction, controlled repetition and drilling, and freer student output activities to define each stage in plain terms. Explain that PPP moves from teacher control toward student independence, and note that the module illustrates this progression through lessons where teachers first present items (e.g., introducing vocabulary with puppets or realia), then guide controlled practice (listen-and-repeat, chants, TPR sequences), and finally invite freer production (games, sentence-making). Do not reference research or studies.

title: The Three Stages of PPP in Detail
brief: Walk through each PPP stage with concrete classroom examples drawn directly from the module. For Presentation, use the module's examples of teachers introducing vocabulary through puppets, realia, and concept-checking questions. For Practice, draw on controlled activities described in the module: listen-and-repeat, chanting at varying speeds, TPR sequences where students perform actions on command, and pointing exercises. For Production, use the module's examples of games such as Hot Potato, hands-on puppet activities, and student sentence-making. Show how each stage has a distinct teacher role and student role, moving from receptive to productive language use.

title: When PPP Fits Best
brief: Describe the lesson contexts in which PPP is a natural fit, drawing on the module's depictions of vocabulary lessons for very young and young learners where new language items are being introduced for the first time. Use the module's examples of warm-up movement activities, TPR songs, and puppet-based vocabulary introduction to show that PPP suits lessons with a clear, discrete target item (a word, a grammar structure, a set phrase). Also draw on the module's discussion of variety—using multiple activity types to reinforce the same target—to explain that PPP works well when the teacher can plan a clear sequence of events with prepared materials. Exclude discussion of Test-Teach-Test, which is covered in the next sections.

title: What Is Test-Teach-Test?
brief: Introduce Test-Teach-Test (TTT) as a framework that reverses the opening move of PPP: students attempt to use language before formal instruction occurs. Draw on the module's descriptions of teachers eliciting student knowledge before explaining it—for example, the teacher who does not tell students what 'photosynthesis' means but instead guides them toward the answer, and the teacher who activates prior knowledge at the start of a science lesson by asking what students already know. Use these examples to define the diagnostic first Test stage, the targeted Teach stage that addresses gaps revealed, and the second Test stage that checks whether the teaching has landed. Do not make claims about research.

title: The Three Stages of TTT in Detail
brief: Explain each TTT stage with classroom-level detail from the module. For the first Test, draw on the module's examples of teachers asking students to display or share knowledge, using assessment conversations with individual students, and eliciting vocabulary meanings through guided questioning rather than direct telling. For the Teach stage, use the module's descriptions of teachers responding to incorrect or absent answers—providing feedback without scolding, smiling, and re-eliciting—and introducing or clarifying only what students could not produce. For the second Test, draw on the module's wrap-up activities and informal assessment moments where teachers check whether objectives were met, including asking comprehension questions and observing student performance. Show how the teacher's role shifts across the three stages.

title: A Worked Mini-Example and Choosing Between the Two Frameworks
brief: Present a single worked mini-lesson that shows both frameworks side by side so a new teacher can see the practical difference. For PPP, build the example from the module's puppet-vocabulary lesson structure: warm-up movement activity → teacher presents two vocabulary items with puppets → controlled chanting and TPR practice → Hot Potato game as freer production. For TTT, build the example from the module's science-lesson structure: teacher asks what students already know about a topic → gaps emerge → teacher introduces the target word and guides students toward its meaning → students demonstrate understanding through questions and display tasks. Close by drawing on the module's discussion of student-centered versus teacher-centered lessons and the value of encouraging student output to help new teachers decide which framework to reach for: PPP when the language item is entirely new; TTT when students may already have partial knowledge worth surfacing first.
